name: Beth Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Beth. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the end of a frozen pizza line, so the flow-wrapper that seals each pizza in film and the case packer that boxes them up. I'm on rotating shifts, two days, two lates, two off. Most of my day is clearing jams, swapping film reels and adjusting the sealing jaws when the film starts wrinkling. When a fault code comes up I take a photo and ask an AI app what it means before I ring the engineer, and nine times out of ten I fix it myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a fault I can't work out at first, it's like a puzzle. The cold is hard, the packing hall is kept at eight degrees and my hands ache by the late shift. And the line speed keeps going up every quarter without anyone asking us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Jo, she's a primary teacher. No partner right now, no kids. I've got about five months saved, partly because I don't drive, I cycle to the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Ha, okay, that'd be a twist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that I still use it every day, it just didn't change the world. Online I'd probably post that the tools are good for small things and the hype was the problem. I'd tell the lads who were scared to relax a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be fine for me. My job's steady, the plant runs three shifts and frozen pizza isn't going out of fashion. The only pressure is the line speed going up, and that's management, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the app for fault codes and keep pushing to get on the engineering apprenticeship the plant runs every September. I'd join the union push against the speed-ups. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more for a trip next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored by the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the apprenticeship, if the job is steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm already doing half the engineer's job for operator pay. If I'm fixing the jaws anyway, I want the title and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned speed-ups. What happens on the line when they push it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More jams, more crushed boxes, more people on the line getting snappy. Last quarter Sam cut his hand clearing a jam because he was rushing.

say: I'd say I still use **AI tools** daily; they just didn't change the world.
I'd tell scared colleagues to **relax** a bit.
think: I think my job is **steady**, because the plant runs three shifts.
I see **line speed-ups** from management as the real pressure.
do: Keep using the **fault code** app every shift.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored by the picture.
S0.quote: I'm already doing half the engineer's job for operator pay.
fieldNote: Beth already uses **AI daily** and sees it as a small, useful tool.
Her ambition is the **engineering apprenticeship**, not escape from the plant.
Her complaint is **line speed**, which she blames on management.

steps.text: Keep photographing fault codes and checking them with the AI app
Apply for the plant's engineering apprenticeship in September
Back the union campaign against line speed-ups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spread more slowly. Okay, I'm with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to grab training while the company still needs us, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. Online I'd post about the apprenticeship and how to apply. I'd also say the union should bargain for retraining time, not just pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is good for me. The planners and the buyers get squeezed, but someone has to keep the wrappers and the robots running. If I'm the person who understands both, I'm worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, and if I didn't get in, I'd pay for an evening course in PLCs myself, that's the controllers that run the line. I'd use AI to study, it's brilliant for explaining wiring diagrams. I'd talk to the engineering manager, Rui, about shadowing on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt about the people in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Jo's mum works in the plant's purchasing team and she's fifty-five. I'd be doing well out of the same thing that pushes my flatmate's mum out of the purchasing office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the evening course cost you, and could you afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine hundred, I think. That's a month and a half of savings, so yes, but it'd sting.

say: I'd urge people to grab **training** while the company still needs us.
I'd say the union should bargain for **retraining time**, not just pay.
think: I think this is **good for me**, because someone must keep the machines running.
Understanding both **wrappers and robots** makes me more valuable.
do: Do the **apprenticeship**, or pay for a PLC evening course myself.
Ask Rui about **shadowing** engineers on days off.
S1.quote: I'd be doing well out of the same thing that pushes my flatmate's mum out of the purchasing office.
fieldNote: Beth sees **opportunity**, not threat, in the slow picture.
Her guilt is personal: her flatmate's **mother** is in purchasing.
She'd spend **savings** on training without hesitation.

steps.text: Pay about nine hundred for an evening PLC course if no apprenticeship
Use AI tools to study wiring diagrams at home
Push the union to bargain for paid retraining time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Wow. Okay, that's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that government has to fund retraining and income support now, not after. At work I'd tell people to learn the robots before the robots learn us. Online I'd be the one posting links to free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's scarier than I'd admit. AGI by 2028 means the AI can diagnose faults better than me, so my party trick goes. The robots that can do my hands-on work come by 2031, so I've got maybe five years where people still need someone to install and fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for robot maintenance hard, apprenticeship or not, and try to get on with the firm that installs the plant's robots. I'd keep two months' savings untouched and spend the rest on courses. I'd also join whatever campaign there is for shared ownership of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit thrilled too, which feels wrong to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Shared ownership of the robots. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot takes my shift, some of what it earns should come back to the people on the line. Like a co-op share. I know it sounds dreamy, but somebody has to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots can fix robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. That's the honest answer. I'd hope by then there's something like a basic income, because I can't out-learn a robot forever.

say: I'd demand **retraining money** and income support from government now, not after.
I'd tell people at work to learn the **robots** before the robots learn us.
think: I think AGI takes my **fault-finding** edge by 2028.
I'd have about **five years** of installing and fixing robots.
do: Apply to the **robot installer** firm that serves the plant.
Spend all but **two months'** savings on courses.
Join the campaign for **shared ownership** of robots.
feel: **Anxious**, and a little **thrilled**, which feels wrong.
S2.quote: I can't out-learn a robot forever.
fieldNote: Beth admits AGI takes her **party trick**: fault diagnosis.
She'd spend most **savings** on training, keeping a small buffer.
Her progressive views show in the **co-op share** idea.

steps.text: Apply to the firm that installs the plant's robots
Spend savings above two months on robot maintenance courses
Join a campaign for workers to share robot earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start now, and I'd say it loudly at the union branch. With friends I'd say this is the moment to retrain. I'd share my study notes online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be well placed. Robots by 2034 gives me time to finish the apprenticeship, get a few years as an engineer and maybe move to the installer side. The thinking part of my job goes in 2031, but I'm not a thinking-job person anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship by 2029 and start building a name with the robot installer. I'd keep saving, maybe aim for eight months. I'd still go to union meetings, because the people on the line need someone who knows the tech on their side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Uneasy about the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam on my line. The man on my line who hates screens is forty, and he'll be the one they let go first. I'd try to drag him to the course with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a thinking-job person. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a hands person. I learn by taking things apart. That's why the three years between AGI and the robots matter so much to me.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if we start now.
I'd share my **study notes** online to help others.
think: I think robots by 2034 give me time to become an **engineer**.
I'm a **hands person**, so the three-year gap protects me.
do: Build a name with the **robot installer**.
feel: Mostly **good**, but **uneasy** about the people around me.
S3.quote: The man on my line who hates screens is forty, and he'll be the one they let go first.
fieldNote: Beth's own path looks safe; her worry is **colleagues** like Sam.
She values the **three-year gap** because her work is hands-on.
She keeps the **union** link as a bridge for less tech-minded workers.

steps.text: Save toward eight months of living costs
Bring Sam from her line to the robot course with her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be stupid to waste it. At work I'd say let's get a training scheme written into the next contract. Online I'd talk about it as a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine with ten years as an engineer behind me. Even if robots fix robots one day, I'd have had time to save, and maybe teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, then an engineering diploma part-time, paid partly by the plant. I'd start saving properly for a flat of my own. I'd help set up a training buddy scheme at the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about what the job looks like then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the training buddy scheme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pair one person who's good with tech with one who isn't, for an hour a week on the clock. I'd pair myself with Sam, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office people still get it first, in 2036. Ten years doesn't help someone who's fifty-five now.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** we mustn't waste.
I'd push for a **training scheme** in the next contract.
think: I think I'd be thirty-nine with **ten years** as an engineer by 2039.
I'd have time to **save** and maybe teach.
do: Do an **engineering diploma** part-time after the apprenticeship.
Save for a **flat** of my own.
Set up a **training buddy** scheme at the plant.
feel: **Calm**, and **curious** about what the job will become.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't help someone who's fifty-five now.
fieldNote: With a long warning Beth is fully **calm** about herself.
Her concern shifts to **older workers** in the office.
The **buddy scheme** shows she thinks in terms of the whole workforce.

steps.text: Take a part-time engineering diploma partly paid by the plant
Save for a deposit on a flat of her own
Set up an hour-a-week training buddy scheme at the plant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge disappears and I'd be racing a clock. What would help is the plant paying for robot training now, and some kind of income floor so people like Sam aren't just dumped.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cold. Nobody wants to stand in an eight-degree packing hall for eight hours, so if a robot does that bit, I won't miss it.

headlineQuote: Nobody wants to stand in an eight-degree packing hall for eight hours, so if a robot does that bit, I won't miss it.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** operator on a frozen pizza packing line, sharing a flat with a friend.
She uses **AI apps** daily to read fault codes and wants an **engineering apprenticeship**.
She sees the slower pictures as a **chance** and spends savings on training.
Her worry is less for herself than for **older colleagues** who dislike screens.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes her anxious, because it removes her fault-finding edge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her edge goes and she'd be racing a **clock**.
whatWouldHelp: The plant paying for **robot training** now, plus an **income floor** for colleagues left behind.
